before: Pick what it stands for on a calm, sober day, so it reminds you of the Nurturer and Protector you've been practicing. And then don't start asking it what to do! It only knows what you knew when you put it there.
after: (Not written yet. The next paragraph, the last of the section: a calm pet can keep you company while you settle, but it's a living animal, not a prop; let them come and go, and don't make them responsible for how it goes. Don't say any of that here.)
brief:
- the guide: "Pair the object with one ordinary promise." The section before already said to pick one thing small enough to repeat (keeping an appointment, eating, going to bed); this is that one thing, written down next to the object.
- the guide's example: "A stuffed animal might sit beside a note saying, 'When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time.'" Keep the note's words close. "Attacking myself" is the article's "internal attack" (calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again); "go to bed on time" meets the end of the section before, where your little one shows up as the one who doesn't want to go to bed.
- the guide: "Symbolic comfort becomes more believable when the Protector follows through." The vow section already says the vow gets believed by what you keep doing ("Watch what I do", "a small thing you keep doing can change their mind"), so don't explain that again; let the note carry it, or a few words at most.
- Don't end on a line that sums it up.
length: two or three sentences, 30 to 60 words
guide_passage: Pair the object with one ordinary promise. A stuffed animal might sit beside a note saying, “When I see you, I remember to stop attacking myself and go to bed on time.” Symbolic comfort becomes more believable when the Protector follows through.
next: A calm pet can offer companionship while you settle, but the animal is a living companion rather than a prop. Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.
